docs#OrdinalApprox.lfpApprox and docs#transfiniteIterate both seem to represent very similar ideas: you take a function, iterate it, and decide on the value at limit points by taking suprema. There are some minor differences:

  • lfpApprox requires a monotone function α →o α. This makes sense to me, as without that and the condition x ≤ f x, taking a supremum at limit points seems unjustified. But we can probably put it in the theorems, rather than the definition.
  • lfpApprox requires a complete lattice. We could weaken all the way to SupSet if we wanted to; I imagine most results will require some kind of lattice anyways.
  • transfiniteIterate indexes by an arbitrary well-order, rather than the ordinals. This might be more convenient but shouldn't change things very much.
  • There is a gfpApprox which takes infima instead of suprema, but no such analog for transfiniteIterate

It seems to me that there is some amount of duplicate work, or at the very least, we have two different ways of writing the same thing. What's the solution here?

Here's my idea:

  • We split transfiniteIterate into supTransfiniteIterate and infTransfiniteIterate. We keep it otherwise unchanged.
  • We deprecate lfpApprox and gfpApprox, and reprove the results about them in terms of these two new definitions.

What do you think? @Joël Riou @Ira Fesefeldt
I do not mind if the current transfiniteIterate is renamed as supTransfiniteIterate and infTransfiniteIterate is added. I have no opinion about lfp/gfpApprox that I am not using.
The lfp/gfp material is only currently used for docs#CantorBendixson.iteratedDerivedSet; it'd be trivial to adapt it to the new infTransfiniteIterate.

I'm wondering if it would even be possible to merge the sup/inf versions. Is there some kind of generalized sequence limit, such that the limit of a monotone increasing sequence is always the supremum when it exists, and the limit of a monotone decreasing sequence is the infimum when it exists?
I think this might be the limsup, or the liminf. Wouldn't really matter. Would this make sense as a way to unify the material?
